title: How to keep up with a fast moving product with a small CE team
summary: Today we dissect how a customer education team of one to three can keep videos and help articles current when the product ships weekly
body_markdown:
Close to half of software teams now release changes to their users every week.


In Google Cloud's[2025 DORA report](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/2025_state_of_ai_assisted_software_development.pdf) , a survey of nearly 5,000 technology professionals, 44.6% said their organization releases at least weekly and 22.7% release daily or more often. The same report found that AI adoption now increases how much software teams deliver, which it didn't the year before. On GitHub, developers made[more than 986 million commits in 2025](https://github.blog/news-insights/octoverse/octoverse-a-new-developer-joins-github-every-second-as-ai-leads-typescript-to-1/) , 25% more than the previous year.


The reason why we're concerned with these numbers is because every release they count also lands on the customer education team. Each change your customer can see needs a help article or video that teaches the new way to use your product. And guess who's responsible for that in most organizations?


Yes, it's customer education, and frankly it's not staffed for this pace. In Thought Industries'[2024 survey of more than 200 customer education teams](https://info.thoughtindustries.com/hubfs/Downloadable%20Content/State%20of%20Customer%20Education%202024/2024%20State%20of%20Customer%20Education%20Report/Thought%20Industries%20-%20State%20of%20Customer%20Education%20Report%202024.pdf) , most of them at software companies, 57% named insufficient headcount among their biggest barriers and 53% said their team was overloaded.


On a team of one or two, the person fixing last week's videos is also the one recording whatever the next release needs. No week is long enough for a team that size to check every video, article, and screenshot against every change.


Small teams that keep up with such velocity do four things differently.


- They decide which changes need any education at all
- They learn about changes before launch day.
- They build flexible content so one product change can be edited retroactively.
- They stop being the only ones who record. Subject matter experts can directly record a process via[Clueso](https://www.clueso.io/) .


## What does it mean for a small team to keep up with weekly releases?


Keeping up with weekly releases means every customer-facing change reaches your help content within a set timeframe and nothing customers rely on shows a screen that no longer exists. For a customer education team of one to three people, that depends on triaging each release, tracking product changes early, and making each update cheaper than the change that caused it.


Small teams often miss this bar, and they know it.


A customer education lead at a financial software company told us the team commits to updating videos within 30 days of a product change, and "we are probably 40% in meeting that." Over two years the company's engineering team grew from 60 people to 350, while the education team went from four people to five.


Video is where the backlog builds. A one-person education team at a revenue-data software company put it plainly. An article takes her 30 minutes to an hour and a video about six hours, "so the documentation is up to date, the videos are usually not."


To size your own gap, take last month's releases, count the videos each one affected, and multiply by the hours a re-record takes you. Compare that with the hours left once new launches and support requests are covered.


## Which releases need a video, which need an article update, and which need nothing?


Ask one question for every item in a release: what does a customer now have to do differently?


If the answer is nothing, the change doesn't need a new video. If they have to find something in a new place, an existing asset needs an edit. New content is only for changes that ask customers to learn something.


What shipped


What the customer has to do differently


What to produce


A new feature or workflow


Learn a task they've never done


A short video and a help article, ready at launch


A moved button, renamed label, or changed screen inside an existing task


Find the same control somewhere else


An edit to the affected step in the article and the video


A new option on an existing screen


Usually nothing, unless it changes the default path


An article update, plus a video edit only if the task now needs the option


A visual refresh of colors, icons, or spacing


Nothing


Your call, made once for the whole library


A bug fix or backend change


Nothing


Nothing beyond the release note


Once you know a change needs an update, decide which asset gets it first. A video and an article rarely cost the same to fix, and they don't do the same job for the customer.


**Update the help article first.** It's what customers find when they search, and it's the quickest asset to correct. A solo instructional designer at a moving-software company, whose product ships every week, works in that order: the help article first, "then it's videos and then it's the courses," and she accepts that courses may run a month or two behind.


**Fix the video in the same release when the change alters how the task is done.** A renamed setting reads fine in text, but a flow that now runs through a new screen is easier to follow by watching it, and a video that still shows the old path sends customers the wrong way. When only a label inside a video changed, the article can go out now and the video edit can follow, because a viewer will still recognize the screen.


**Update nothing when the clicks are the same and the screen is still recognizable.** That covers bug fixes, backend changes, and small spacing tweaks. Within the assets that do need work, start with the ones customers reach most often, such as those linked from onboarding emails, in-app help, or your top help center searches, and leave rarely viewed ones for a later pass.


Visual overhauls are the hard case, because the clicks stay the same while every screen looks different. A one-person technical content team decided a rebrand from teal to orange didn't justify re-recording 111 videos: "enough has to be different to warrant the effort." A two-person team at a fleet-management company reached the opposite conclusion when a sidebar went from blue to green, which "instantly outdated our videos." That team reviews its change log quarterly, and with releases going out constantly, "the list is growing." When every fix means a manual re-record, skipping the update is often the only realistic call for a small team.

## How do you find out what's changing before it ships?


Many small teams first see a change on launch day, once the screens are finished and there's no time left to plan. Triage, drafting, and recording then all have to happen in the same few days. We’ve discovered these four habits move most of that work earlier.


**Ask for the change list before the build exists.** Triage doesn't need finished screens. It needs to know what's changing, and that list sits in product's tickets and release-note drafts days before the build reaches a test account. Ask for it while it's still being drafted and sort each item through the table above, so launch week goes on producing content rather than deciding what to produce. Some teams go further and work with product operations to feed release notes straight into their content pipeline.


**Draft from whatever product can show you.** A heads-up from a product manager and a few prototype screenshots are enough to outline the help article and decide which steps the video will show. The spec is enough to start the launch video: Clueso builds a narrated video with[motion graphics](https://www.clueso.io/features/motion-graphics) from a prompt, a script, a document, or a slide deck, so the feature overview can be ready before the build is, and the walkthrough clip goes in once the screens exist.


**Let the code tell you what changed.** On the Enterprise plan, connecting your frontend GitHub repository lets Clueso Agents read each product change, draft scripts from it, and suggest videos for new flows that don't have one yet. You can also trigger a video directly from your release workflow, so the first draft of a new-feature video starts from the release itself rather than from someone remembering to tell you.


**Catch the changes nobody wrote down.** Release notes tend to miss the small changes, and a renamed label rarely makes them at all. Finding every video that shows the old label used to mean walking each changed screen by hand. With the repository connected, the agent works out which product flows each release changed and lists the videos that now show an outdated screen. You accept or dismiss each one, so the triage call stays yours. Without a connected repository, walking the changed areas in a test account is still the safest check, and our post on[keeping help center articles current](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-to-automatically-update-help-center-articles) covers how to find the articles a release breaks.

## How do you build videos so a weekly change takes minutes instead of a re-record?


When every product change means a re-record, each new video adds to the upkeep, so small teams end up making fewer of them. The fix is to make an update cheap enough that video is worth making again, and that depends on how each video is built.


**Scope each video to one task.** A two-minute video on inviting a teammate goes stale only when the invite flow changes. A 20-minute product tour goes stale with almost every release, and fixing it means finding the right minute first. Our[AI playbook for customer education teams](https://www.clueso.io/blog/7-ai-moves-for-customer-education-teams) covers cutting one long recording into short videos.


**Keep the narration as text.** When the narration is a human recording, a renamed label means getting the same person back to the same microphone. Clueso turns your rough narration into a clean script and generates the[AI voiceover](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) from it, so the editable text exists from the first draft. A renamed label becomes a one-line script edit and a regenerated voiceover for that one clip.


**Get the article from the same project.** Clueso writes a[step-by-step help article](https://www.clueso.io/features/help-articles) alongside the video, with screenshots taken from it, and can rewrite the article from the updated video after an edit. One update reaches both, and the article can't drift away from the video.


**Describe the edit instead of making it.** On the Enterprise plan, you can tell[Clueso Agents](https://www.clueso.io/features/clueso-agents) what changed, such as "the Export button is now called Download", and the agent updates the script line, voiceover, and callouts in the existing video without regenerating the rest. Every change can be reverted from version history.


**Put the look in a template.** An updated clip should match the clips around it without anyone matching fonts by eye. A[Clueprint](https://www.clueso.io/features/clueprints) holds your brand, layout, and editing style, so brand decisions happen once rather than once per video, and every clip an update produces comes out matching.

## How does a team of one stop being the only person who records?


When the education team records and narrates everything, its calendar sets the limit on how much help content the company gets. As the product grows, the team also can't stay expert in every part of it. Two changes take most of the recording off its plate.


**Hand recording to the people who know the feature.** Product managers and support leads already know what changed and how the new flow works. Ask them for a rough recording in a test account with the[Clueso screen recorder](https://www.clueso.io/features/screen-recorder) , narrated the way they'd walk a customer through it on a call, and tell them not to restart when they stumble. Clueso turns their narration into a clean script and voiceover and adds the zooms and callouts. Your team keeps the parts that need one owner: triage, templates, review, and publishing.


**Let an agent record the routine flows.** Some flows don't need a person at the keyboard at all. On the Enterprise plan, the browser agent in[Clueso Agents](https://www.clueso.io/agents) logs into your product, follows a prompt or a written walkthrough step by step, and records the flow. Clueso then adds the voiceover, zooms, callouts, and brand styling, and returns an editable draft that your team reviews like any other video before it ships. ## How do you measure whether your content keeps up with releases?


Measure the days between a release and the updated content, counted only for the changes your triage said needed an update. Set a target, such as 30 days, and track the share of updates that meet it. Without that number, a small team only learns it's behind when customers start asking about screens that no longer exist.


Then watch support. In a[2024 Gartner survey of 5,728 customers](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2024-08-19-gartner-survey-finds-only-14-percent-of-customer-service-issues-are-fully-resolved-in-self-service) , 73% used self-service at some point, but only 14% of issues were fully resolved there. In 43% of failed attempts, customers couldn't find content relevant to their issue, and a help article that teaches an old screen is one way that happens. A ticket that quotes an old label, or asks where a button went the week after it moved, points at the asset to fix next. ## Frequently asked questions


### How can I keep up with creating videos for every sprint release without hiring a video team?


Triage each release so only new workflows get new videos, keep each video to one task, and generate narration from a script so updates are edits. ### Our product changes constantly and our tutorial videos go stale. How do teams handle re-recording at scale?


Re-record as little as possible. Fix the label or narration when that's all that changed, swap only the affected step when a screen changed, and group the remaining re-records by screen so one session fixes every video that shows it. In Clueso, you edit a clip's script and regenerate its voiceover, restore earlier versions from version history, and embedded videos update in place when you republish. On the Enterprise plan, you can describe the change to[Clueso Agents](https://www.clueso.io/features/clueso-agents) and the agent edits the script, voiceover, and callouts without regenerating the rest of the video. With your GitHub repository connected, the agents also find the videos a release has made outdated and regenerate them when you accept the update, and[Auto Updates](https://www.clueso.io/pricing) , an Enterprise add-on, re-runs an existing guide against the current product and regenerates the steps that changed.


### Is there software that detects when help center articles are outdated?


Yes, if the software can see your code. On the Enterprise plan,[Clueso Agents](https://www.clueso.io/agents) connect to your frontend GitHub repository, detect product changes with each release, and identify the videos and guides that now show an outdated screen. Each one comes back as a suggested update you can accept, which regenerates it, or dismiss. Because Clueso writes the help article from the same project as the video, the article updates with it. Without a connected repository, teams work from the release instead: list what changed, search articles and video transcripts for the old labels, and walk the changed screens to catch what the notes missed. Our post on[updating help center articles automatically](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-to-automatically-update-help-center-articles) covers that workflow.


### What should a customer education team look for in a tool to produce several videos a week?


Judge what an update costs, not only what a first video costs. Check that narration comes from an editable script, that one recording produces both the video and the article, that templates hold your brand across authors, and that a changed step can be replaced without re-recording. Then check how much of the update work the tool takes off you: whether it can find the videos a release broke, and whether it can make an edit from a plain-language instruction.
